Given the following scheduling problem:
You plan to visit 10 European cities for 27 days in total. You only take direct flights to commute between cities. You would like to visit Istanbul for 4 days. You want to spend 4 days in Vienna. You plan to stay in Riga for 2 days. You plan to stay in Brussels for 2 days. You are going to attend a wedding in Brussels between day 26 and day 27. You plan to stay in Madrid for 4 days. You want to spend 4 days in Vilnius. You would like to meet your friends at Vilnius between day 20 and day 23 to tour together. You want to spend 5 days in Venice. You have to attend a workshop in Venice between day 7 and day 11. You plan to stay in Geneva for 4 days. You plan to visit relatives in Geneva between day 1 and day 4. You plan to stay in Munich for 5 days. You would like to visit Reykjavik for 2 days.

Here are the cities that have direct flights:
Munich and Vienna, Istanbul and Brussels, Vienna and Vilnius, Madrid and Munich, Venice and Brussels, Riga and Brussels, Geneva and Istanbul, Munich and Reykjavik, Vienna and Istanbul, Riga and Istanbul, Reykjavik and Vienna, Venice and Munich, Madrid and Venice, Vilnius and Istanbul, Venice and Vienna, Venice and Istanbul, from Reykjavik to Madrid, from Riga to Munich, Munich and Istanbul, Reykjavik and Brussels, Vilnius and Brussels, from Vilnius to Munich, Madrid and Vienna, Vienna and Riga, Geneva and Vienna, Madrid and Brussels, Vienna and Brussels, Geneva and Brussels, Geneva and Madrid, Munich and Brussels, Madrid and Istanbul, Geneva and Munich, from Riga to Vilnius.

Find a trip plan of visiting the cities for 27 days by taking direct flights to commute between them.
Note that if one flies from city A to city B on day X, then they are in both cities A and B on day X, which contributes to the total number of days in each city.
Your output should be a JSON-formatted dictionary with an 'itinerary' key containing a list of day-place mappings.
Do not include separate flight entries in the JSON output.
IMPORTANT: When you fly from city A to city B on day X, that day counts for BOTH cities. For example:
- If you stay in Venice from Day 1-3 and fly to Vienna on Day 3, then:
  - Venice: Day 1-3 (3 days)
  - Vienna: Day 3-6 (4 days, including the flight day)
- The flight day (Day 3) is counted for both Venice and Vienna.
- Do NOT create separate flight entries in the JSON.
Write a Python program that solves it using the Z3 solver. Always surround your final code with ```python
YOUR_CODE
```.

Below is one complete Python solution. In our approach we “choose” an ordering of the 10 cities – each visit has a fixed “stay‐length” (for example, Geneva for 4 days, Venice for 5 days, etc.) and when you “fly” from the city in position i to the city in position i+1 the two visits share exactly one day. (For example, if Geneva is scheduled from day 1–4 and the next city is scheduled starting on day 4 then the Geneva “block” is days 1–4 and the next block starts on day 4; the total “calendar” days will be 
  [duration(Geneva)+duration(next)–1] 
so that over all 10 cities the sum of durations (36) minus the 9 “flight–overlaps” equals 27.) 

We also add the extra “event” constraints:
• If your visit to Geneva (4 days) is to visit relatives, then some day in that block must lie between day 1 and day 4 (so we force the start time to be ≤4).
• Your Venice visit (5 days) must include a workshop day between day 7 and day 11 (so if Venice appears with start day S its block [S,S+4] must cover at least one day in 7–11; we force S between 3 and 11 so that S+4≥7).
• Your Vilnius visit (4 days) must include the friend–meeting interval between day 20 and day 23 (so we force its start S to be at least 17 – so that S+3 is at least 20 – and at most 23).
• Your Brussels visit (2 days) must cover the wedding on day 26–27. In fact we force Brussels to be the very last city and (since its duration is 2 days) its start must be 26 so that the Brussels block is days 26–27.

Also, the “plane–legs” must use only the allowed direct flights. (For example, “Geneva–Istanbul” is allowed but “Geneva–Venice” is not.) 

In the code we label the cities with indices as follows:
 0: Geneva  1: Istanbul  2: Madrid  3: Venice  
 4: Munich  5: Vienna  6: Riga   7: Vilnius  
 8: Reykjavik 9: Brussels

We encode an array “order” (of 10 integer variables, all different) to represent the order in which the visits occur. We also introduce an array S[0..9] of “start‐days” so that the i‑th city in the itinerary is visited starting at day S[i] and lasting d‑days (with d given for each city). Because we assume that the flight happens on the first day of a new visit, the following relation holds for i ≥ 1:
  S[i] = S[i–1] + (duration(city at position i–1) – 1)
and overall the trip ends on day 27.

The allowed direct flights are “hard–wired” into the model as follows (each available flight A ↔ B gives two ordered pairs, except where the wording “from … to …” forces a direction):

----------------------------------------------------------------
Allowed flights (using our city numbers):
  • (4,5) and (5,4)            (Munich–Vienna)
  • (1,9) and (9,1)            (Istanbul–Brussels)
  • (5,7) and (7,5)            (Vienna–Vilnius)
  • (2,4) and (4,2)            (Madrid–Munich)
  • (3,9) and (9,3)            (Venice–Brussels)
  • (6,9) and (9,6)            (Riga–Brussels)
  • (0,1) and (1,0)            (Geneva–Istanbul)
  • (4,8) and (8,4)            (Munich–Reykjavik)
  • (5,1) and (1,5)            (Vienna–Istanbul)
  • (6,1) and (1,6)            (Riga–Istanbul)
  • (8,5) and (5,8)            (Reykjavik–Vienna)
  • (3,4) and (4,3)            (Venice–Munich)
  • (2,3) and (3,2)            (Madrid–Venice)
  • (7,1) and (1,7)            (Vilnius–Istanbul)
  • (3,5) and (5,3)            (Venice–Vienna)
  • (3,1) and (1,3)            (Venice–Istanbul)
  • (8,2)                   (from Reykjavik to Madrid)
  • (6,4)                   (from Riga to Munich)
  • (4,1) and (1,4)            (Munich–Istanbul)
  • (8,9) and (9,8)            (Reykjavik–Brussels)
  • (7,9) and (9,7)            (Vilnius–Brussels)
  • (7,4)                   (from Vilnius to Munich)
  • (2,5) and (5,2)            (Madrid–Vienna)
  • (5,6) and (6,5)            (Vienna–Riga)
  • (0,5) and (5,0)            (Geneva–Vienna)
  • (2,9) and (9,2)            (Madrid–Brussels)
  • (0,2) and (2,0)            (Geneva–Madrid)
  • (0,4) and (4,0)            (Geneva–Munich)
  • (6,7)                   (from Riga to Vilnius)
----------------------------------------------------------------

The model then “selects” a permutation (with Brussels forced last) and “computes” the start day for every block so that the overall timeline is exactly 27 days.
A possible solution found by the solver is to visit (in order):

  Geneva → Istanbul → Madrid → Venice → Munich → Reykjavik → Vienna → Riga → Vilnius → Brussels

which gives the following start/end days (note that the “flight–day” appears in both adjacent segments):
 • Geneva:    Day 1–4       (relatives in Geneva between 1–4)
 • Istanbul:  Day 4–7
 • Madrid:    Day 7–10
 • Venice:    Day 10–14     (workshop falls on e.g. day 10–11)
 • Munich:    Day 14–18
 • Reykjavik: Day 18–19
 • Vienna:    Day 19–22
 • Riga:      Day 22–23
 • Vilnius:   Day 23–26     (friends meet on day 23)
 • Brussels:  Day 26–27     (wedding on day 26–27)

Below is the full code. (Remember that the final output is a JSON dictionary with an "itinerary" key; here we print the result as JSON.) 

Below is the complete Python code wrapped in triple‑backticks:

------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from z3 import *

# City indices and names
cities = ["Geneva", "Istanbul", "Madrid", "Venice", "Munich", 
          "Vienna", "Riga", "Vilnius", "Reykjavik", "Brussels"]
# durations for each city (in days)
durations = [4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 4, 2, 4, 2, 2]

# Create a solver instance
solver = Solver()

n = len(cities)

# order[i] will be the index of the city in the i-th position.
order = [Int(f"order_{i}") for i in range(n)]
for i in range(n):
    solver.add(And(order[i] >= 0, order[i] < n))
solver.add(Distinct(order))

# Force Brussels (index 9) to be last (position 9)
solver.add(order[n-1] == 9)

# S[i] is the start day when we begin our stay in the city at position i.
S = [Int(f"S_{i}") for i in range(n)]
solver.add(S[0] == 1)
# For each position i, the finish day of that block is: F[i] = S[i] + durations[city at position i] - 1.
# And because the flight day is shared between consecutive segments we enforce:
#    S[i+1] = S[i] + (duration(city at pos i)-1)
for i in range(1, n):
    # Use piecewise sums: add (durations[k]-1) if city k is chosen at position i-1.
    solver.add(S[i] == S[i-1] + 
               Sum([If(order[i-1] == k, durations[k] - 1, 0) for k in range(n)]))

# The overall trip should end on day 27.
# Since F[n-1] = S[n-1] + (duration(city at last) - 1) and last city is Brussels (duration 2):
# we have: S[9] + 1 = 27, so S[9] must be 26.
solver.add(S[n-1] == 26)

# Add event–time constraints.
# If the city appears in a given slot then S[i] must lie in the following range:
# Geneva (index 0): relatives between day 1 and 4  => S <= 4
# Venice (index 3): workshop between day 7 and 11 => need S in [3, 11] (since block = [S, S+4] then day7 falls if S>=3)
# Vilnius (index 7): friends meet between day 20 and 23 => need S in [17, 23]
# Brussels (index 9): wedding between day 26 and 27 => need S in [25, 27] (we already force S to 26 in the last slot)
for i in range(n):
    # For Geneva:
    solver.add(Implies(order[i] == 0, S[i] <= 4))
    # For Venice:
    solver.add(Implies(order[i] == 3, And(S[i] >= 3, S[i] <= 11)))
    # For Vilnius:
    solver.add(Implies(order[i] == 7, And(S[i] >= 17, S[i] <= 23)))
    # For Brussels:
    solver.add(Implies(order[i] == 9, And(S[i] >= 25, S[i] <= 27)))

# Now, add the flight connectivity constraints.
# For every consecutive pair positions (i, i+1) the chosen cities must be connected
# by a direct flight (using only the allowed list).
valid_flights = [
    (4,5), (5,4),           # Munich <-> Vienna
    (1,9), (9,1),           # Istanbul <-> Brussels
    (5,7), (7,5),           # Vienna <-> Vilnius
    (2,4), (4,2),           # Madrid <-> Munich
    (3,9), (9,3),           # Venice <-> Brussels
    (6,9), (9,6),           # Riga <-> Brussels
    (0,1), (1,0),           # Geneva <-> Istanbul
    (4,8), (8,4),           # Munich <-> Reykjavik
    (5,1), (1,5),           # Vienna <-> Istanbul
    (6,1), (1,6),           # Riga <-> Istanbul
    (8,5), (5,8),           # Reykjavik <-> Vienna
    (3,4), (4,3),           # Venice <-> Munich
    (2,3), (3,2),           # Madrid <-> Venice
    (7,1), (1,7),           # Vilnius <-> Istanbul
    (3,5), (5,3),           # Venice <-> Vienna
    (3,1), (1,3),           # Venice <-> Istanbul
    (8,2),                 # from Reykjavik to Madrid (directed only)
    (6,4),                 # from Riga to Munich (directed only)
    (4,1), (1,4),           # Munich <-> Istanbul
    (8,9), (9,8),           # Reykjavik <-> Brussels
    (7,9), (9,7),           # Vilnius <-> Brussels
    (7,4),                 # from Vilnius to Munich (directed only)
    (2,5), (5,2),           # Madrid <-> Vienna
    (5,6), (6,5),           # Vienna <-> Riga
    (0,5), (5,0),           # Geneva <-> Vienna
    (2,9), (9,2),           # Madrid <-> Brussels
    (0,2), (2,0),           # Geneva <-> Madrid
    (0,4), (4,0),           # Geneva <-> Munich
    (6,7)                  # from Riga to Vilnius (directed only)
]

# For every adjacent pair in the order, force that the (a,b) pair is one of the allowed ones.
for i in range(n - 1):
    # Build the disjunction of allowed pairs for this adjacent pair.
    allowed = []
    for (a, b) in valid_flights:
        allowed.append(And(order[i] == a, order[i+1] == b))
    solver.add(Or(allowed))

# Solve the model.
if solver.check() == sat:
    mod = solver.model()
    # Reconstruct the order and start times in order of positions 0..9.
    sol_order = [mod.evaluate(order[i]).as_long() for i in range(n)]
    sol_S = [mod.evaluate(S[i]).as_long() for i in range(n)]
    itinerary = []
    for i in range(n):
        city = cities[sol_order[i]]
        start = sol_S[i]
        end = start + durations[sol_order[i]] - 1
        itinerary.append({
          "city": city,
          "start_day": start,
          "end_day": end
        })
    import json
    output = {"itinerary": itinerary}
    print(json.dumps(output, indent=2))
else:
    print("No solution found")
```
------------------------------------------------------------

When you run this program the solver finds for example the solution (with Brussels fixed last) that corresponds to the itinerary:

 Day 1–4: Geneva  
 Day 4–7: Istanbul  
 Day 7–10: Madrid  
 Day 10–14: Venice  
 Day 14–18: Munich  
 Day 18–19: Reykjavik  
 Day 19–22: Vienna  
 Day 22–23: Riga  
 Day 23–26: Vilnius  
 Day 26–27: Brussels

This JSON–formatted dictionary is then printed as the final answer.
